one_liner: WASM-SIMD (optionally multi-threaded) hashes and ciphers from Paul Miller; BLAKE3 about 8-19x single-threaded throughput of @noble/hashes in reported runs.
what_it_does: A single npm/JSR package (@awasm/noble, v0.1.4) with SHA-1/2/3, Keccak/SHAKE, BLAKE1/2/3, RIPEMD-160, MD5, HMAC, HKDF, PBKDF2, scrypt, Argon2, ChaCha/Salsa (+Poly1305), AES (GCM, GCM-SIV, SIV, CTR, CBC, CFB, OFB, ECB, KW) and GHASH/POLYVAL/CMAC. The API follows the noble libraries (hash(msg), .create().update().digest(), .chunks(), .parallel(), .async()), with a few deliberate differences: cmac takes (msg, key), stream ciphers use cipher(key, nonce).encrypt/decrypt, and some noble features (kmac, cshake, turboshake, ff1, PRNGs) are absent. The same source compiles to six interchangeable backends (wasm, wasm_threads, js, runtime, plus noble and webcrypto wrappers), and stub.js lets a library ship one function whose backend the application swaps at run time.
how_it_is_fast: Algorithms are written in a JS-embedded DSL and compiled by awasm-compiler to WebAssembly with 128-bit SIMD; batchFn lays out state so SIMD lanes process independent blocks: separate messages for SHA/MD/BLAKE2 (multi-buffer hashing, which is why .parallel()/.chunks() matter), and independent 1 KB chunks of one input for BLAKE3, whose Merkle tree is then folded by a parent-compression stack. The wasm_threads backend adds a Web Worker pool driven by Atomics on shared memory instead of postMessage, so BLAKE3 and parallelisable cipher modes (CTR, ECB, ChaCha20, the encryption half of GCM/SIV) split one large input across workers, and other hashes spread multiple inputs. The baseline @noble/hashes is scalar pure JavaScript, so the gain is SIMD plus wasm's predictable 32/64-bit integer code rather than a new algorithm.
when_to_use: Browser or Node/Bun/Deno code that hashes large buffers with BLAKE3 (file checksums, content addressing) and cannot use a native addon: about 1.9 GB/s single-threaded on Apple M4 versus about 0.1 GB/s for @noble/hashes.
Hashing many independent messages at once (Merkle leaves, dedup indexes) with .parallel() or .chunks(), where multi-buffer SIMD and the worker pool apply even to SHA-256, SHA-512, SHA-3 and BLAKE2.
Bulk ChaCha20/XChaCha20-Poly1305 or AES-CTR/GCM encryption of megabyte-scale data in the browser where WebCrypto is unavailable, async-only or lacks the mode (XChaCha, GCM-SIV, AES-SIV, KW).
Libraries that want a noble-compatible API today and an opt-in faster backend later: stub.js plus the noble.js wrapper lets the application decide.
Pages that already serve COOP/COEP headers (cross-origin isolated) and can afford the worker pool, for the threaded multi-GB/s figures.
when_not_to_use: Server-side Node for SHA-2/SHA-1/MD5 where node:crypto (OpenSSL) is available: the package's own harness benchmarks against node:crypto but publishes no result, and its single-threaded wasm SHA-256 figure is 553 MB/s on Apple M4.

Strict CSP environments: the wasm backends need 'wasm-unsafe-eval', and wasm_threads needs Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin plus Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp; without them use the js or noble backend and lose the speedup.
Small messages: at 32 B the reported gain over @noble/hashes is only 3.1-3.75x, the threaded backend is no faster (94 vs 105 MB/s on M4), and blake3-wasm-rs was faster at 32 B on both CPUs.

Code that must resist cache-timing attacks with AES or GHASH: the AES rounds use T-table lookups (T0..T3 plus S-box tables, lanes fixed at 1) and GHASH uses precomputed tables; wasm has no AES or carry-less-multiply instructions.

Projects that need audited code or a stable API: version 0.1.x, about 50 commits, no published audit (the noble libraries it wraps are audited; this package is not), and SECURITY.md points to a README Security section that does not exist.

integration.dependencies: none at run time for the wasm/js backends (wasm binaries are embedded as base64 in JS); optional peers @noble/hashes 2.4.0 and @noble/ciphers 2.4.0 (noble.js backend) and @awasm/compiler 0.1.5 (runtime backend)
integration.min_toolchain: Node.js >= 22.22.0 (package.json engines); Bun and Deno supported; browsers with WebAssembly SIMD, plus SharedArrayBuffer and Atomics for wasm_threads
integration.platforms: any WebAssembly-SIMD runtime (browsers, Node, Bun, Deno, Vercel example included); wasm_threads needs cross-origin isolation in browsers
integration.thread_safety: not documented beyond the threaded backend: one shared worker pool (bitmask of up to 31 workers) per process; Deno needs WP.stop() to exit because workers lack unref
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same call shapes as @noble/hashes for hashes (hash(msg), create/update/digest), but import paths differ, async methods are hash.async rather than hashAsync, cmac and stream-cipher signatures differ from @noble/ciphers, and some noble functions (kmac, cshake, turboshake, kt128, ff1, PRNGs) are missing

gotchas: Correctness history: version 0.1.0 returned wrong BLAKE3 digests, silently, in the wasm and wasm_threads backends for input lengths in [4096k-63, 4096k-2] (62 lengths per 4 KiB band, about 1.5% of sizes) because a SIMD lane mask truncated the last-block length to its low bit (PR #2, fixed in 0.1.1 on 2026-04-20); the js backend and streaming path were unaffected. PR #1 fixed streaming digests ignoring create()'s dkLen. Pin >= 0.1.1 and cross-check against @noble/hashes in tests.

Provenance of the comparison: the Apple M4 table in UneBaguette/blake3.wasm (the source of the 8-19x figures) was added by awasm-noble's own author in PR #1 there (2026-04-22, 'readme: add awasm-noble entry'), so those numbers are first-party; only the Ryzen 7 5800X table comes from the blake3-wasm-rs author. The table's columns and sizes (32 B, 1 KB, 64 KB, 1 MB, 10 MB; old noble, wasm, threads, blake3-wasm-rs) match awasm-noble's benchmark/internal/hashes.ts, but no run log is published. In the M4 table the blake3-wasm cells at 64 KB (2,004) and 1 MB (1,893) are identical to that column in the earlier Ryzen table, so that column may be partly copied. The measured sizes fall outside the 0.1.0 bug's affected lengths.

README Speed section is stale relative to its scripts: it says 'input: 32x1mb' and 'blake3 1x100mb' and 'ciphers, input: 1gb', while benchmark/2-parallel.ts uses 48 chunks, a 1x1gb BLAKE3 case and 10 MB cipher inputs; its multi-input hash figures (e.g. sha1 11,413 MB/s, blake3 11,058 MB/s) feed the same 1 MB buffer 48 times (Array(48).fill(data)), so the data stays cache-resident and the numbers are an upper bound for 48 distinct inputs. The M4 figures also predate the 'Improve perf of single-shot hashes' (2026-06-13) and new-compiler (2026-07-20) commits.

Synchronous by default even with threads; the README does not say how a synchronous threaded call waits on a browser main thread, so test UI responsiveness and use the .async variants for large inputs.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over hash-wasm when you need BLAKE3 or AEAD ciphers at multi-GB/s with optional worker threads, multi-input .parallel() hashing, a noble-compatible API with swappable backends, or reproducible wasm built from auditable JS source; hash-wasm is the more established single-threaded wasm hash library and fast-noble-hashes targets SHA-2 against @noble/hashes. For small BLAKE3 inputs in Node, blake3-jit reports wins over a native addon, which awasm-noble does not claim.
verified_claims_summary: Only BLAKE3 has a baseline comparison: in the blake3.wasm README (Node.js v24, measured with constant-filled buffers in what appears to be awasm-noble's own comparison harness), awasm-noble's single-threaded wasm backend did 843/1,898/1,943 MB/s at 1 KB/64 KB/1 MB versus 105/102/101 MB/s for pure-JS @noble/hashes on Apple M4 (rows contributed by awasm-noble's author), and 1,729 vs 52 MB/s at 64 KB on a Ryzen 7 5800X (run by the blake3-wasm-rs author); worker-thread figures reach 4.7-6.5 GB/s. awasm-noble's own README gives absolute Apple M4 numbers only (blake3 1,940 MB/s single-threaded, 6-11 GB/s threaded) with no baseline.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-09-12, v0.1.4, 52 stars, MIT, sole maintainer with a strong track record from the audited noble libraries), but pre-1.0, unaudited and with a BLAKE3 wrong-digest bug fixed only in 0.1.1, so pin versions and keep cross-checks; copyable as an npm/JSR dependency.
